_notes: Review loop. Anne-marie Greene confirmed the 20-minute interval and estimated one hour per act. Published curtain times are loaded; house-opening times are copied from Popcorn for confirmation. Two separated anchors repeat the complete content notice. The supplied wording retains strobe while Paul Harrison confirms strobe versus flashing lights. Brontë material and the director wording are approved for this review. Bar, ice-cream and sound content revised 10 September 2026: the single bar slide is replaced by a rotating pool of five multi-panel bar montages, so the cards rarely repeat across a preshow hour. Named stock is draft pending the bar team; the guest ale is deliberately not named because it rotates.

content.headline: CONTENT NOTICE
content.body: This production contains explicit language, themes of grief and death, and a depiction of an attempted suicide. Staging involves use of haze and strobe effects. Suitable for ages 14 and above. The Criterion advises caution but does not enforce an age limit.

items._note: Cast list from the Criterion production page. Image-free table; no headshots needed.

content.quote: Everyone knows Wuthering Heights. Everyone knows Jane Eyre. This is a play about the Brontë sister you can't quite name — and about what her family did to make sure of that.

content.headline: Three sisters. Three pen names.
content.body: Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell: Charlotte, Emily and Anne published as men, keeping their initials.

content.headline: Two novels. An uncompromising voice.
content.body: Anne wrote Agnes Grey (1847) and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848). Her second novel was a hit.

content.headline: A sister's verdict
content.body: After Anne died, Charlotte opposed a new edition of The Tenant of Wildfell Hall. It remained out of print for years.

content.headline: The {other} other one
content.body: Anne died in Scarborough in 1849, aged 29. Her writing still asks difficult questions.

content.headline: Not just a bonnet drama
content.body: “The Brontës meets Fleabag”: the Nick Darke Award judges on Sarah Gordon's prize-winning script, 2020.
